READING

**The gate that matters**

Everything turns on the four weeks ending 2027-02-28. Pass then and the grant flows from April; miss and there is a five-to-six-month gap before August offers a second chance. During that gap the station runs on reserve with no grant income and either a £21,000 coordinator or a £20,280 Halverston contract still running. The reserve stands at £62,000 and fixed costs plus whichever commitment is chosen come to roughly £79,000 a year, so the burn in a gap period is about £6,500 a month. Five months of that erases roughly £32,500, leaving perhaps £29,000 of reserve when the grant finally starts — thin but not fatal. The question is therefore which course gives the higher probability of passing in February rather than August, because the cost of missing February is severe even if survivable.

**Hours: ELSWICK passes with certainty, CRANMOOR carries real execution risk**

ELSWICK contracts six hours a week from Halverston from 5 October 2026. Added to the nine the station already carries, that is fifteen hours — one clear of the mark, on a signed agreement, from well before the assessment window opens. The commissioned-content ceiling is 40 % (6 out of 15), comfortably inside the 50 % limit.

CRANMOOR must close the same gap through volunteers. The brief puts the additional recruitment needed at roughly fifteen contributors. In all of 2025, without a coordinator, the station added nine — about 0.75 a month gross. To reach fifteen new people on air within the five months from a coordinator's 1 October start requires something between three and four times the historical intake rate. Critically, the pipeline is not instant: induction and training typically take four to six weeks before a new contributor is broadcasting regularly, so contributors recruited in October may not add measurable hours until December at the earliest. The usable window before the assessment period begins in February is closer to three months of productive scheduling, not five. The net contributor count has also been falling (41 in 2024, 34 today), which means churn continues to eat into any recruitment gains. A capable coordinator could transform this picture, but the February deadline requires transforming it very fast. The probability of reaching 14 hours by the assessment is genuinely uncertain — my estimate is somewhere between 35 % and 50 %. That is a meaningful chance of failure.

**Contributor register: both courses probably hold, but CRANMOOR holds more safely**

The station needs 30 registered contributors on 28 February 2027 and currently holds 34. The net decline has averaged roughly 3–4 a year, suggesting a six-month drift to perhaps 32–33 — above the floor. Under ELSWICK, Halverston's producers do not join the register, so no recruitment benefit flows from the commission; but the existing team has managed to add nine contributors in a year before, and a modest effort from within the 1.6-post paid staff should be enough to hold above 30.

Under CRANMOOR the coordinator works the register directly, which should slow churn as well as drive new entrants. Either way the contributor criterion looks more likely to hold than not under both courses, though CRANMOOR is the safer option here.

**Financial analysis**

Both costs fall inside the board cap (£22,000). ELSWICK at £20,280 and CRANMOOR at £21,000 are almost identical in year one.

The divergence is in what happens if February is missed under each option.

— ELSWICK missing February (contributor register falls below 30): probability low, maybe 10–15 %. If it happens, the gap cost is similar to CRANMOOR's scenario, but reserve enters Local Voice at roughly £58,000.

— CRANMOOR missing February (hours short): probability 50–65 %. Reserve entering the gap at £62,000 exits the gap at roughly £25,000. That is workable but leaves almost no margin for anything else in year one of the grant.

There is also a structural financial issue with ELSWICK over the longer term: under the Local Voice grant of £96,000, fixed costs of £58,000 leave £38,000 for programming commitments. Halverston at £20,280 leaves only £17,720 — not enough to add a coordinator at £21,000 without simultaneously cutting Halverston's hours. Breaking out of Halverston dependency requires having enough volunteers to carry the hours before you can afford to redirect the money. That is a viable but awkward transition. Under CRANMOOR, if February is reached, the coordinator is already in place and the programming is owned; the grant surplus of roughly £17,000 is available for contingencies rather than being locked into a contract.

**Summary of the asymmetry**

ELSWICK almost certainly passes February on hours, leaves the reserve largely intact, but creates a structural dependency that is hard to unwind within the Local Voice budget.

CRANMOOR offers better long-term sustainability but carries a majority-weighted risk of missing the February assessment, with a reserve consequence that is serious though survivable.

The February gate is the decisive event. Missing it costs roughly £37,000 in reserve under CRANMOOR; failing to pass it under ELSWICK is much less probable. The difference in execution risk — certain vs roughly coin-flip — on the most consequential single outcome is large enough to outweigh CRANMOOR's long-term advantages, especially when the reserve entering a potentially stretched year-one of Local Voice matters so much to the station's resilience.

---

CALL
ELSWICK

---

GROUNDS
CRANMOOR requires recruiting approximately fifteen volunteer contributors and building them to air within five months, a pace three to four times the station's historical rate and too uncertain a foundation on which to risk a February failure that would drain roughly £37,000 of the £62,000 reserve in the gap period; ELSWICK delivers the required fifteen hours on contract from the outset with near-certain passage of the February assessment.
